explanation: Recess is the period between the prorogation of a House and its reassembly in a new session; adjournment ends only a sitting and prorogation ends the session.

notes.text: - **Session**: first sitting → prorogation/dissolution. **Recess**: the period between **prorogation** and the reassembly in a new session.

q: A sitting of the Parliament can be terminated by adjournment, prorogation or dissolution. In this regard choose the correct answer.
options: Prorogation terminates the session of Parliament
Adjournment sine die means terminating a sitting for an indefinite period
key_text: Adjournment sine die means terminating a sitting for an indefinite period
explanation:
APPSC key: (c) adjournment sine die. Strictly, (a) 'prorogation terminates the session' and (b) 'dissolution terminates only the Lok Sabha' are also true (NextGen Polity p.363; Laxmikanth ch. Parliament).
Adjournment sine die means terminating a sitting of Parliament for an indefinite period – the APPSC key. Option (d) is clearly wrong: adjournment never ends a session.

notes.text: - APPSC G1 2018: "adjournment sine die = terminating a sitting for an indefinite period" (key); prorogation ends the session; dissolution applies only to the LS; adjournment **never** ends a session.

q: In India, if motion of thanks to President's address is defeated, then who would resign?
explanation: Defeat of the Motion of Thanks on the President's address means the Government has lost the confidence of the Lok Sabha, so the Government (PM and Council of Ministers) must resign – not the President or Speaker.

notes.text: - The address is **prepared by the Union Cabinet** (it states the Government's policy) and is debated on a **Motion of Thanks**; defeat of the Motion of Thanks = defeat of the **Government**, which must **resign**.

q: Normally how many sessions of the Lok Sabha are held in a year?
explanation: Parliament normally meets in three sessions a year – Budget, Monsoon and Winter; Art. 85 only says six months may not pass between sessions (so at least two).

notes.text: - **Three sessions** – **Budget** (Feb-May, **longest**), **Monsoon** (Jul-Sep), **Winter** (Nov-Dec, **shortest**) – a **convention**, not in the Constitution; no fixed number of sessions or minimum sitting days is laid down. States: **Art. 174** (same six-month rule); State Assemblies averaged only **24 sittings in 2025**.

q: What is the quorum for Lok Sabha meetings?
explanation: The quorum of either House is one-tenth of its total membership (Art. 100(3)), which for the Lok Sabha is about 55 members.

notes.text: - **Quorum**: **one-tenth** of the total members of the House, **including the presiding officer** – **Art. 100(3)**.

q: The time gap between two sessions of Parliament is not more than:
explanation: Art. 85: not more than six months may pass between two sessions of Parliament (Art. 174 has the same rule for State Legislatures).

notes.text: - **Art. 85(1)**: the **President summons** each House (separately or together) at such time and place as he thinks fit, but **six months shall not intervene** between the **last sitting of one session** and the **first sitting of the next** → Parliament must meet **at least twice a year**.
- **Gap between two sessions** – "shall not exceed **six months**" (flashcard).
